summary: Gives reasons for a reasonably large default MTU for IP over ATM AAL5 and presents the default value to use. It was a standards-track proposal. It was replaced by RFC 2225.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1626 sets a default maximum size for IP packets carried over ATM AAL5. The value is 9180 octets, chosen to support large frames and reduce fragmentation; RFC 2225 later replaced this memo.

questions: what is the default ip mtu for atm aal5
how big should packets be on atm networks
subtitle: A default IP packet size for use over ATM AAL5.

tldr.problem: Large application frames can be split into IP fragments, which the RFC says is undesirable and can reduce performance.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets the default IP MTU for ATM AAL5 to 9180 octets and describes how switched virtual circuits negotiate their sizes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1626 was obsoleted by RFC 2225. Its default is specified in this memo as 9180 octets.

sections.title: Why Use a Large Default MTU
sections.content:
Applications such as NFS use large frames. The RFC notes that NFS defaults to an 8192-byte frame and would prefer an MTU of at least 8300 octets after accounting for its protocol headers. Fragmenting IP datagrams is undesirable, and routers can sometimes perform better with larger packets because many costs relate to packets handled rather than bytes transferred.

The RFC chooses the same default used for IP over SMDS to support interoperability and reduce fragmentation.
sections.plainLanguage: Large application frames may need to be split if the network's packet limit is too small. A larger default can reduce that splitting and the work it creates.

sections.title: The Default IP MTU
sections.content:
The default IP MTU for ATM AAL5 is 9180 octets. All implementations conforming to the specification must support at least that default.

For Permanent Virtual Circuits, implementations use the default unless both parties have agreed in advance to another value through a mechanism outside this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Use 9180 octets as the default packet limit for IP over ATM AAL5. Systems must support at least that value.

sections.title: Agreeing on a Size for Switched Circuits
sections.content:
Implementations that support Switched Virtual Circuits must try to negotiate the AAL CPCS-SDU size using ATM signalling. The SETUP message carries proposed sizes in the AAL Parameters information element, and the called endpoint responds in CONNECT. The forward and backward sizes can differ.

If an endpoint receives data units larger than the negotiated MTU, it may fragment the IP packet or clear the call. The RFC also requires router implementations to implement Path MTU Discovery and says hosts should implement it.
sections.plainLanguage: Switched circuits agree on packet sizes when they connect, and the two directions may use different sizes. Routers must support Path MTU Discovery so IP can account for different network limits.

sections.title: Applicability and Status
sections.content: The RFC says its rules apply generally to models of IP over ATM AAL5 and recommends using them to improve interoperability and performance. It states that the memo does not discuss security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo applies to different ways of carrying IP over ATM AAL5. It was later obsoleted by RFC 2225.
